plain.text: Paul turns to people who judge others. When you judge someone else, you condemn yourself, because you do the same things. Do you think you will escape God's judgement? Or do you look down on God's kindness, patience and tolerance, not realising that his kindness is meant to lead you to turn back to him? God will repay each person according to what they have done. He will give eternal life to those who keep doing good and seek glory, honour and immortality. But for those who are selfish and reject the truth, there will be anger and trouble. God does not show favouritism.

Those who sin without having God's law will be judged without the law, and those who have the law will be judged by it. It is not those who hear the law who are right with God, but those who obey it. Even Gentiles who do not have the law sometimes do by nature what the law requires, showing that its demands are written on their hearts; their consciences agree. This will be shown on the day God judges people's secrets through Jesus Christ.

Paul then addresses those who call themselves Jews, rely on the law and boast in God, and who teach others. "You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?" Breaking the law dishonours God. Circumcision has value if you obey the law, but if you break it, it is as though you were not circumcised. A person is not a Jew merely on the outside, by physical circumcision. Rather, a true Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit. Such a person's praise comes from God, not people.

summary.bigIdea: God judges everyone fairly, without favouritism, and looks at the heart rather than outward signs.
points: Judging others while doing the same things is self-condemning.
God's kindness is meant to lead people to turn back to him.
What matters to God is a changed heart, not just outward religion.
summary.reflection: Paul says God's kindness leads us to turn back to him. Where have you seen God's kindness in your life?
